title: Motion to suppress evidence
content: California Penal Code section 1538.5 authorizes a defendant to move for the return of property or to suppress evidence obtained as a result of an unreasonable search or seizure. A motion under this section may be made to challenge a search or seizure conducted without a warrant, or with a warrant alleged to be insufficient on its face, or where there is no probable cause for the issuance of the warrant, or where the property or evidence obtained is not that described in the warrant, or where there was not a substantial basis for the magistrate to find probable cause. The section sets procedures for noticing the motion, the hearing, and the effect of a grant or denial on later proceedings.

title: Murder defined
content: California Penal Code section 187 defines murder as the unlawful killing of a human being, or a fetus, with malice aforethought. Express malice is when there is manifested a deliberate intention unlawfully to take away the life of a fellow creature. Implied malice is when no considerable provocation appears, or when the circumstances attending the killing show an abandoned and malignant heart. The section is the primary definition used with related homicide and special-circumstance statutes.

title: Robbery defined
content: California Penal Code section 211 defines robbery as the felonious taking of personal property in the possession of another, from his person or immediate presence, and against his will, accomplished by means of force or fear. Robbery is a specific-intent crime requiring intent to permanently deprive. Degrees and sentencing enhancements are addressed in related sections.

title: Burglary
content: California Penal Code section 459 provides that every person who enters any house, room, apartment, tenement, shop, warehouse, store, mill, barn, stable, outhouse or other building, tent, vessel, floating home, railroad car, locked or sealed cargo container, trailer coach, house car, inhabited camper, vehicle, aircraft, mine or any underground portion thereof, with intent to commit grand or petit larceny or any felony is guilty of burglary. Entry with the requisite intent is the core of the offense.

title: Theft defined
content: California Penal Code section 484 defines theft to include the felonious stealing, taking, carrying, leading, or driving away of the personal property of another, or fraudulently appropriating property entrusted, or obtaining property by false pretenses. Related sections distinguish grand theft and petty theft and set value thresholds and punishments.

title: Resisting, delaying, or obstructing an officer
content: California Penal Code section 148 makes it unlawful to willfully resist, delay, or obstruct any public officer, peace officer, or emergency medical technician in the discharge or attempt to discharge any duty of that office. The statute has been interpreted to require that the officer be engaged in the lawful performance of duties. Related subdivisions address removing or taking an officer's firearm or weapon.

title: Diversion of defendants with controlled substance issues
content: California Penal Code section 1000 and following sections authorize deferred entry of judgment or diversion programs for certain controlled substance offenses when statutory eligibility criteria are met. Successful completion can result in dismissal of charges. Eligibility, notice, and court procedures are detailed in the statutory scheme.

title: Initial appearance
content: Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 5 governs the initial appearance of a defendant after arrest. A person making an arrest within the United States must take the defendant without unnecessary delay before a magistrate judge. The rule addresses informing the defendant of the complaint and right to counsel, detention or release, and preliminary hearing scheduling.

title: Pleadings and pretrial motions
content: Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 12 addresses pleadings and pretrial motions. Rule 12(b)(3) lists defenses, objections, and requests that must be raised by pretrial motion if the basis is then reasonably available, including defects in instituting the prosecution, defects in the indictment or information, and suppression of evidence. Failure to raise a required motion can result in waiver subject to the rule's exceptions.

title: Discovery and inspection
content: Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 16 governs discovery and inspection in criminal cases. Upon a defendant's request, the government must disclose items within its possession, custody, or control that are material to preparing the defense, intended for use in its case-in-chief, or were obtained from or belong to the defendant, subject to listed categories and limitations. Reciprocal discovery obligations and continuing duty to disclose also apply.

title: Search and seizure
content: Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 41 addresses search and seizure warrants, including authority to issue a warrant, contents of the warrant, execution and return, and motions for return of property. The rule interacts with Fourth Amendment standards requiring probable cause supported by oath or affirmation and particularity as to the place to be searched and the persons or things to be seized.

title: Speedy Trial Act time limits
content: 18 U.S.C. § 3161 sets time limits under the Speedy Trial Act. Any information or indictment charging an individual with an offense shall be filed within thirty days from the date on which the individual was arrested or served with a summons in connection with such charges. Trial shall commence within seventy days from the filing date of the information or indictment, or from the date the defendant has appeared before a judicial officer of the court in which the charge is pending, whichever date last occurs, subject to exclusions in the statute.

title: Miranda v. Arizona
content: Holding-level summary: Prior to any custodial interrogation, a person must be warned that he has a right to remain silent, that any statement he does make may be used as evidence against him, and that he has a right to the presence of an attorney, either retained or appointed. Failure to give adequate warnings generally renders statements obtained during custodial interrogation inadmissible in the prosecution's case-in-chief, subject to later doctrinal developments.

title: Brady v. Maryland
content: Holding-level summary: The suppression by the prosecution of evidence favorable to an accused upon request violates due process where the evidence is material either to guilt or to punishment, irrespective of the good faith or bad faith of the prosecution. Brady obligations extend to evidence that is material and favorable, including impeachment evidence under later cases.

title: Brown v. Board of Education (illustrative citation practice)
content: Educational note for citation practice only: Landmark equal protection decision concerning segregation in public education. Included in the seed corpus to exercise hybrid retrieval on well-known federal citations; not a substitute for full reporter text.

title: Rape defined
content: California Penal Code section 261 defines rape as an act of sexual intercourse accomplished with a person not the spouse of the perpetrator under enumerated circumstances including where a person is incapable of giving legal consent, where it is accomplished against a person's will by means of force, violence, duress, menace, or fear of immediate and unlawful bodily injury, or where a person is prevented from resisting by intoxication or unconsciousness.

title: Criminal threats
content: California Penal Code section 422 makes it a crime to willfully threaten to commit a crime which will result in death or great bodily injury to another person, with the specific intent that the statement is to be taken as a threat, even if there is no intent of actually carrying it out, when the threat on its face and under the circumstances is so unequivocal, unconditional, immediate, and specific as to convey a gravity of purpose and an immediate prospect of execution, causing the victim reasonably to be in sustained fear.

title: Disorderly conduct
content: California Penal Code section 647 defines disorderly conduct offenses including soliciting or engaging in lewd or dissolute conduct in public, loitering, public intoxication, and related misdemeanors. Subdivisions address specific fact patterns and penalties.

title: Probation
content: California Penal Code section 1203 governs probation, including eligibility, investigation reports, terms and conditions, and revocation procedures. Courts may grant probation in lieu of a sentence in appropriate cases subject to statutory limits.

title: Determinate sentencing
content: California Penal Code section 1170 sets determinate sentencing rules for felonies, including selection of lower, middle, or upper terms and findings required for aggravating circumstances following legislative reforms.

title: First degree murder
content: Arizona Revised Statutes section 13-1105 defines first degree murder, including intentional or knowing killing with premeditation and felony-murder theories enumerated in the statute. Classification and sentencing implications follow related capital and noncapital provisions.

title: Aggravated assault
content: Arizona Revised Statutes section 13-1204 defines aggravated assault, elevating assault when specified factors are present such as serious physical injury, use of a deadly weapon or dangerous instrument, or assault on protected classes of victims including peace officers.

title: Theft
content: Arizona Revised Statutes section 13-1802 defines theft, including controlling property of another with intent to deprive, converting lost property, and obtaining property by misrepresentation. Degree and classification depend on value and circumstances.

title: Arrest without warrant by officer
content: Arizona Revised Statutes section 13-3883 authorizes a peace officer to arrest a person without a warrant when the officer has probable cause to believe a felony has been committed and the person committed it, or for misdemeanors committed in the officer's presence, subject to statutory conditions.

title: Motion to return property or suppress evidence
content: Arizona Revised Statutes section 13-3925 provides procedures for a person aggrieved by an unlawful search and seizure to move for return of property and to suppress its use as evidence. The motion is heard by the court and may result in restoration of property and exclusion of evidence if the search or seizure was unlawful.

title: Deprivation of rights under color of law
content: 18 U.S.C. § 242 makes it a federal crime for a person acting under color of any law to willfully subject any person to the deprivation of any rights, privileges, or immunities secured or protected by the Constitution or laws of the United States. Penalties increase when bodily injury or death results.

title: False statements
content: 18 U.S.C. § 1001 prohibits knowingly and willfully falsifying, concealing, or covering up a material fact, or making any materially false statement or representation, in any matter within the jurisdiction of the executive, legislative, or judicial branch of the United States government.

title: Tampering with a witness, victim, or informant
content: 18 U.S.C. § 1512 criminalizes killing or attempting to kill, using physical force or threats, or otherwise corruptly persuading another person with intent to influence, delay, or prevent testimony or production of evidence in an official proceeding.

title: Admissibility of confessions
content: 18 U.S.C. § 3501 addresses admissibility of confessions in federal criminal prosecutions, directing courts to determine voluntariness considering the totality of circumstances. Application is constrained by constitutional doctrine including Miranda.

title: Test for relevant evidence
content: Federal Rule of Evidence 401 provides that evidence is relevant if it has any tendency to make a fact more or less probable than it would be without the evidence, and the fact is of consequence in determining the action.

title: Excluding relevant evidence for prejudice, confusion, waste of time, or other reasons
content: Federal Rule of Evidence 403 allows the court to exclude relevant evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by a danger of unfair prejudice, confusing the issues, misleading the jury, undue delay, wasting time, or needlessly presenting cumulative evidence.

title: Testimony by expert witnesses
content: Federal Rule of Evidence 702 governs expert witness testimony, requiring that the expert's scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge will help the trier of fact, the testimony is based on sufficient facts or data, is the product of reliable principles and methods, and the expert has reliably applied the principles and methods to the facts of the case.

title: United States v. Leon
content: Holding-level summary: The Fourth Amendment exclusionary rule does not bar the use in the prosecution's case in chief of evidence obtained by officers acting in reasonable reliance on a search warrant issued by a detached and neutral magistrate but ultimately found to be unsupported by probable cause. The good-faith exception is subject to limitations where the magistrate was misled, wholly abandoned the judicial role, the affidavit was so lacking in probable cause as to render official belief unreasonable, or the warrant was facially deficient.

title: Terry v. Ohio
content: Holding-level summary: Where a police officer observes unusual conduct which leads him reasonably to conclude in light of his experience that criminal activity may be afoot and that the persons with whom he is dealing may be armed and presently dangerous, he is entitled for the protection of himself and others in the area to conduct a carefully limited search of the outer clothing in an attempt to discover weapons.

title: Coolidge v. New Hampshire
content: Holding-level summary: Addresses warrant requirements and exceptions including plain view. For the plain-view doctrine, the officer must be lawfully present, the item's incriminating character must be immediately apparent, and discovery must be consistent with lawful presence; later cases refine inadvertence requirements.
